{{Short description|none}}
{{Numeral systems}}
{{Contains special characters|Burmese}}
'''[[Burmese language|Burmese]] numerals''' ({{langx|my|မြန်မာ ကိန်းဂဏန်းများ}}, {{IPA|my|mjàɰ̃mà kéiɰ̃ ɡa̰náɰ̃ mjá}}) are a set of [[Numeral (linguistics)|numeral]]s traditionally used in the [[Burmese language|<span lang="my" dir="ltr">Burmese language</span>]], although [[Arabic numerals]] are also used. Burmese numerals follow the [[Hindu–Arabic numeral system]] commonly used in the rest of the world.

==Main numbers==
[[File:Script styles of Burmese numerals.svg|thumb|Burmese numerals in various script styles (from the equivalent of zero to nine)]]

===Zero to ten===
The Burmese numerals from 1 to 10 are all etymologically traced back to the [[Proto-Sino-Tibetan language]], with shared cognates in related languages like Tibetan and Chinese.

<sup>1</sup> Burmese for ''[[0 (number)|zero]]'' comes from [[Sanskrit]] śūnya.<br/>
<sup>2</sup> Can be abbreviated to {{IPA|my|kʰʊ̀ɰ̃|IPA}} in list contexts, such as telephone numbers.

Spoken Burmese has innate pronunciation rules that govern numbers when they are combined with another word, be it a numerical place (e.g. tens, hundreds, thousands, etc.) or a measure word.<ref name="bbe">{{cite book|last=Okell|first=John|title=Burmese By Ear|publisher=The School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London|date=2002|isbn=186013758X|url=http://www.soas.ac.uk/bbe/file53735.pdf|access-date=2015-01-21|archive-date=2021-04-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210420002442/https://www.soas.ac.uk/bbe/file53735.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

* For one, two, and seven (all of which end in the rhyme {{IPA|[-ɪʔ]}}), when combined, shift to an open vowel, namely the schwa ({{IPA|[ə]}})
* For three, four, five, and nine which all have the long tone (similar to the [[Standard Chinese phonology#Tones|first tone in Mandarin Chinese]]), when combined, the word immediately following it, given that it begins with a consonant, shifts to a [[voiced consonant]] (e.g., {{lang|my|၄၀}}, "40" is pronounced {{IPA|[lé zɛ̀]}}, not {{IPA|[lé sʰɛ̀]}}). Other suffixes such as {{lang|my|ထောင်}} ({{IPA|[tʰàʊɰ̃]}};  thousand), {{lang|my|သောင်း}} ({{IPA|[θáʊɰ̃]}};  ten thousand), {{lang|my|သိန်း}} ({{IPA|[θéɪɰ̃]}}; hundred thousand), and {{lang|my|သန်း}} ({{IPA|[θáɰ̃]}}; million) all shift to ({{IPA|[dàʊɰ̃]}};  thousand), ({{IPA|[ðáʊɰ̃]}};  ten thousand), ({{IPA|[ðéɪɰ̃]}}; hundred thousand), and {{IPA|[ðáɰ̃]}}; million), respectively.
* For six and eight, no pronunciation shift occurs.

These pronunciation shifts are exclusively confined to spoken Burmese and are not spelt any differently.

===Ten to a million===
While the Burmese numbers from 'hundred' to 'ten thousand' are etymologically traced back to the [[Proto-Sino-Tibetan language]], the numbers for 'hundred thousand' may be an areal word. The numbers beyond 'million' are derived from Pali.

<sup>2</sup> Athinche ({{lang|my|အသင်္ချေ}}) sometimes could mean "too large to be counted".

Ten to nineteen are almost always expressed without including {{lang|my|တစ်}} (one).

Another pronunciation rule shifts numerical place name (the tens, hundreds and thousands place) from the low tone to the creaky tone.<ref name="bbe"/>
*Number places from 10 ({{lang|my|တစ်ဆယ်}}) up to 10<sup>7</sup> ({{lang|my|ကုဋေ}}) has increment of 10<sup>1</sup>. Beyond those Number places, larger number places have increment of 10<sup>7</sup>. 10<sup>14</sup> ({{lang|my|ကောဋိ}}) up to 10<sup>140</sup> ({{lang|my|အသင်္ချေ}}) has increment of 10<sup>7</sup>.
*There are totally 27 major number places in Burmese numerals from 1×10<sup>0</sup> to 10<sup>140</sup>
*Numbers in the tens place: shift from {{lang|my|ဆယ်}} ({{IPA|[sʰɛ̀]}}, low tone) to {{lang|my|ဆယ့်}} ({{IPA|[sʰɛ̰]}}, creaky tone), except in numbers divisible by ten (10, 20, 30, etc.) In typical speech, the shift goes farther to ({{IPA|[sʰɛʔ]}} or {{IPA|[zɛʔ]}}).
*Numbers in the hundreds place: shift from {{lang|my|ရာ}} ({{IPA|[jà]}}, low tone) to {{lang|my|ရာ့}} ({{IPA|[ja̰]}}, creaky tone), except for numbers divisible by 100.
*Numbers in the thousands place: shift from {{lang|my|ထောင်}} ({{IPA|[tʰàʊɰ̃]}}, low tone) to {{lang|my|ထောင့်}} ({{IPA|[tʰa̰ʊɰ̃]}}, creaky tone), except for numbers divisible by 1000.
Hence, a number like 301 is pronounced {{IPA|[θóʊɰ̃ ja̰ tɪʔ]}} ({{lang|my|သုံးရာ့တစ်}}), while 300 is pronounced {{IPA|[θóʊɰ̃ jà]}} ({{lang|my|သုံးရာ}}).

The digits of a number are expressed in order of decreasing digits place. For example, 1,234,567 is expressed as follows (where the highlighted portions represent numbers whose tone has shifted from low → creaky:

<sup>1</sup> When combined with the numeral place, the pronunciations for 1 and 2 shift from a checked tone (glottal stop) to an open vowel ({{IPA|[ə]}}).

====Round number rule====
When a number is used as an adjective, the standard word order is number + measure word:

{{fs interlinear|lang=my|indent=2|glossing2=yes|italics2=no|italics3=no
|'''၅''' ခွက်
|'''five''' CL
|''''5''' cups'
}}

In spoken Burmese, for [[round number]]s (numbers ending in zeroes), the word order is flipped to measure word + number:<ref name="cb">{{cite book|author=San San Hnin Tun|title=Colloquial Burmese: The Complete Course for Beginners|publisher=Routledge|date=2014}}</ref> 

{{fs interlinear|lang=my|indent=2|glossing2=yes|italics2=no|italics3=no
|ခွက် '''၂၀'''
|CL '''twenty'''
|''''20''' cups'
}}

The exception to this rule is the number 10, which follows the standard word order.<ref name="bbe"/>
{{fs interlinear|lang=my|indent=2|glossing2=yes|italics2=no|italics3=no
|'''၁၀''' ခွက် 
|'''ten''' CL
|''''10''' cups'
}}

===Ordinal numbers===
Ordinal numbers, from first to tenth, are Burmese pronunciations of their [[Pali]] equivalents.<ref name="bbe"/> They are prefixed to the noun. Beyond that, cardinal numbers can be raised to the ordinal by suffixing the particle {{lang|my|မြောက်}} ({{IPA|[mjaʊʔ]}}, {{lit|to raise}}) to the number in the following order: number + [[Burmese numerical classifiers|measure word]] + {{lang|my|မြောက်}}.

===Decimal and fractional numbers===
Colloquially, decimal numbers are formed by saying {{lang|my|ဒသမ}} ({{IPA|[daʔθəma̰]}}, Pali for 'tenth') where the [[decimal separator]] is located:

{{fs interlinear|lang=my|indent=2
|ဆယ် ဒသမ တစ်
|ten decimal one
|'10.1'
}}

Half (1/2) is expressed primarily by {{lang|my|တစ်ဝက်}} ({{IPA|[təwɛʔ]}}), although {{lang|my|ထက်ဝက်}}, {{lang|my|အခွဲ}} and {{lang|my|အခြမ်း}} are also used. Quarter (1/4) is expressed with {{lang|my|အစိတ်}} ({{IPA|[ʔəseɪʔ]}}) or {{lang|my|တစ်စိတ်}}. Other fractional numbers are verbally expressed as follows: denominator + {{lang|my|ပုံ}} ({{IPA|[pòʊɰ̃]}}) + numerator + {{lang|my|ပုံ}} ({{lit|portion}}):

{{fs interlinear|lang=my|indent=2
|လေး ပုံ သုံး ပုံ
|four portions three portions
|'3/4'
}}

===Alternate numbers===
Other numbers, not of Tibeto-Burman origin, are also found in the Burmese language, usually from [[Pali]] or [[Sanskrit]].<ref name="hlape">{{cite book|last=Hla Pe|title=Burma: Literature, Historiography, Scholarship, Language, Life, and Buddhism|publisher=Institute of Southeast Asian Studies|date=1985|pages=64|isbn=9789971988005}}</ref> They are exceedingly rare in modern usage.

===Abbreviations===
To indicate prices of merchandise, a circle is placed above the final zero of the price and a slash is added to indicate currency:<ref>{{Cite book |last=Jenny |first=Mathias |title=Burmese: a comprehensive grammar |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |others=San San Hnin Tun |isbn=978-0-415-73569-8 |series=Routledge comprehensive grammars |location=London New York}}</ref>

:'2,500': ၂၅၀၀ိ/ = $၂၅၀၀
